newsitem.title: UK: UK Treasury Committee urges further reforms at LSE.
newsitem.headline: UK Treasury Committee urges further reforms at LSE.

text.p: An influential Parliamentary committee on Thursday urged the London Stock Exchange (LSE) to adopt a corporate structure.
The Treasury Select Committee, which has been critical of the way the exchange is run, said the LSE would better reflect the interests of the market if it was not owned by member firms.

"It is apparent that the LSE is increasingly being run as a business rather than a co-operative," the Committee said it its report. "We can see no reason why the Stock Exchange should now not develop a corporate structure."

The Committee said it was concerned that the exchange is "remains so non-committal about the issue of ownership, particularly in the light of the increasingly competitive environment in which it finds itself."
It added, "...We would not be surprised if the LSE came under further scrutiny from this Committee in the new Parliament."
The LSE declined to comment immediately, saying it was still reviewing the report.
The Committee also urged Europe's biggest stock exchange to increase the transparency of markets with the October 20 launch of the electronic order-driven order book.
The LSE currently uses a system under which share prices are set by primary dealers, known as market makers. It is the only major exchange where share prices are set by market makers.
The LSE has put forth a controversial rule that would allow market makers to delay reporting large trades for the sake of market liquidity under the new order book regime.
"...We do not accept the view of the LSE that there is necessarily a trade off between transparency and liquidity," the committee reported.

It concluded, "...The LSE will be best served by ensuring that an effective, transparent order book -- with suitably formulated rules to allow a significant flow of business -- for the most liquid stocks is implemented as soon as possible ..."
